guides.title: Reading difficulties
guides.concern: A learner often reads words differently from what is written.
observable_behaviours: Reads a different vowel sound (hat as hit).
Leaves off word endings (dig for digs).
Skips small words or whole lines.
Reads slowly and tires quickly.
context_questions: Does this happen with unfamiliar words or with all words?
Is the learner reading in their home language?
Was the room noisy or was the learner tired?
alternative_explanations: The words or language are unfamiliar.
The print is small or the page is crowded.
The learner is tired, anxious, or distracted.
Instructions were unclear.
things_to_try_now: Try chunked text or sound-by-sound pointing from the support catalogue.
Pre-teach 3 to 4 hard words before reading.
Record a baseline with Form A and compare with a matched follow-up.
what_to_record: Which words were read differently, exactly as heard.
Whether the pattern repeats across two attempts.
What support was tried and for how long.
guides.how_to_judge: Compare words read as written on matched passages before and after the support, with the careful wording on the comparison screen.
guides.when_to_seek_help: If the pattern is sustained across attempts plus your observations, consider discussing it with a qualified professional.
guides.non_diagnostic_statement: MINDTRACE gives educational observations, not diagnoses.

guides.title: Attention and executive function
guides.concern: A learner struggles to start, stay with, or finish a task.
observable_behaviours: Starts quickly then stops partway.
Loses their place or repeats steps.
Seems to forget the instruction midway.
context_questions: How long was the task, and how many steps did it have?
What time of day was it?
Did a shorter version go better?
alternative_explanations: The task was long or had many steps.
The learner was tired or hungry.
The instructions were given all at once.
The format did not suit them.
things_to_try_now: Give one step at a time with extra processing time.
Shorten the task and add a visible break.
Let the learner respond in a different format.
what_to_record: How long the learner stayed with the task, in minutes.
Which step they reached before stopping.
What changed when the task was shortened.
guides.how_to_judge: Compare completion on the same task shape before and after the change.
guides.when_to_seek_help: If difficulty persists across settings and strategies, consider discussing it with a qualified professional.
guides.non_diagnostic_statement: MINDTRACE gives educational observations, not diagnoses.

guides.title: Learning in a second or additional language
guides.concern: A learner who speaks another language at home makes consistent sound-pattern errors in English reading.
observable_behaviours: Substitutes sounds that do not exist in the home language.
Reads fluently in the home language but hesitates in English.
Understands the story when it is discussed but stumbles reading it.
context_questions: Which languages does the learner speak at home?
How long have they been learning in English?
Do the errors follow a consistent sound pattern?
alternative_explanations: The sound pattern is unfamiliar, not a reading barrier.
Vocabulary in the passage is new.
The learner has had less time with English print.
things_to_try_now: Pre-teach vocabulary with pictures before reading.
Use listen-then-read so the sounds are heard first.
Check understanding by discussion, not only by reading aloud.
what_to_record: Home language and time learning in English.
Which sound patterns repeat.
Whether discussion shows the content is understood.
guides.how_to_judge: Look for the pattern across attempts and check it against the home-language explanation first.
guides.when_to_seek_help: If difficulty persists in all languages the learner uses, consider discussing it with a qualified professional.
guides.non_diagnostic_statement: MINDTRACE gives educational observations, not diagnoses.

guides.title: Predictability, sensory and communication needs (autism-related patterns)
guides.concern: A learner shows heightened distress during unplanned transitions, reacts strongly to sensory stimuli, or communicates best with visual supports.
observable_behaviours: Becomes visibly unsettled or stops participating when the classroom schedule changes without notice.
Covers ears, squints, or withdraws during noisy group work or under bright fluorescent lighting.
Follows instructions significantly better when accompanied by pictures or physical demonstrations than by verbal commands alone.
Repeats phrases verbatim (echolalia) or prefers solitary, predictable play during breaks.
context_questions: Did distress coincide with high classroom noise, crowded spaces, or sudden routine changes?
Was the instruction delivered verbally in a busy room without visual cues?
Does the learner engage comfortably when activities follow a consistent, expected sequence?
alternative_explanations: The classroom environment has high acoustic reverberation or visual clutter.
The learner was caught off guard by an unannounced activity switch.
Verbal explanations were too rapid or contained complex figurative language.
things_to_try_now: Use a visual schedule with picture cards showing the order of activities.
Give a 5-minute and a 2-minute verbal or visual warning before switching tasks.
Provide a quiet workspace corner or permit noise-reducing headphones during independent reading.
Pair verbal instructions with concrete visual cues.
what_to_record: Which specific environmental triggers preceded distress (noise level, lighting, task change).
Whether task engagement changed after introducing a visual timetable.
Which communication format elicited the clearest responses.
guides.how_to_judge: Track task completion and signs of ease across one week with the visual schedule versus the prior baseline.
guides.when_to_seek_help: If significant sensory distress or communication barriers persist despite accommodations, discuss observations with a SENCo or qualified educational psychologist.
guides.non_diagnostic_statement: MINDTRACE gives educational observations, not diagnoses.

guides.title: Mathematics and number relationships (dyscalculia-related patterns)
guides.concern: A learner experiences persistent difficulty with basic number concepts, magnitude comparison, or place-value calculations.
observable_behaviours: Struggles to identify which quantity is larger without counting every single item one by one.
Reverses or inverts digits in multi-digit numbers (writing 42 for 24).
Consistently subtracts the smaller digit from the larger regardless of column position (e.g. 52 - 17 = 45).
Has difficulty estimating position on a 0 to 20 number line.
Relies heavily on finger counting for simple additions well past the expected stage.
context_questions: Does difficulty increase when numbers are presented purely as abstract symbols rather than concrete objects?
Has the learner mastered basic one-to-one counting principles?
Does the layout of the math worksheet cause visual crowding or misalignment?
alternative_explanations: Working memory overload from multi-step written arithmetic.
Lack of prior experience with concrete math manipulatives.
Spatial confusion caused by crowded worksheets without clear columns.
things_to_try_now: Use physical manipulatives (base-10 blocks, bead strings, counters) before writing numbers.
Provide colour-coded columns for units, tens, and hundreds on arithmetic tasks.
Use visual spatial number lines with landmarks at 5, 10, and 15.
Allow extra processing time and oral explanation of math reasoning.
what_to_record: Specific error patterns in multi-digit operations (e.g. column swaps, direction of subtraction).
Difference in accuracy when using physical counters versus written digits alone.
Response time and strategy used for quantity comparisons.
guides.how_to_judge: Compare accuracy and confidence on comparable 10-item math sets with and without physical manipulatives.
guides.when_to_seek_help: If persistent difficulties with basic number sense and magnitude endure after sustained structured support, consider consulting a specialist.
guides.non_diagnostic_statement: MINDTRACE gives educational observations, not diagnoses.

guides.title: Speech sound production and expressive language
guides.concern: A learner experiences difficulty producing clear speech sounds or structuring spoken sentences.
observable_behaviours: Consistently omits or substitutes specific consonant sounds in spoken words.
Understands complex stories but responds with one- or two-word phrases.
Demonstrates hesitation or word-finding pauses when describing everyday events.
context_questions: Does the learner communicate with greater fluency in their home language?
Has the learner recently had a hearing or middle-ear check?
Does speech clarity improve in quiet, one-on-one conversation?
alternative_explanations: Temporary hearing attenuation from middle-ear fluid (glue ear).
Second-language acquisition process (silent period or developmental sound approximations).
Performance anxiety when speaking in front of peers.
things_to_try_now: Model correct sound production gently without asking for forced repetition.
Allow alternative response formats such as pointing, drawing, or gesture.
Ensure clear face-to-face visual contact when speaking.
Provide extra wait time (5 to 8 seconds) before expecting a spoken answer.
what_to_record: Which specific sound clusters or words show consistent substitutions.
Language used at home and age of first exposure to the language of instruction.
Observations of listening and comprehension in quiet versus noisy rooms.
guides.how_to_judge: Observe whether clarity and communicative confidence increase with one-to-one wait time over two weeks.
guides.when_to_seek_help: If speech clarity severely impedes peer understanding or persists across settings, consider a referral to a speech and language therapist.
guides.non_diagnostic_statement: MINDTRACE gives educational observations, not diagnoses.

guides.title: Writing demands, fine motor, and letter formation
guides.concern: A learner demonstrates severe fatigue, pain, or illegibility during handwriting tasks.
observable_behaviours: Holds pencil with an unusually tight, awkward grip and presses heavily into the page.
Expresses thoughts orally with rich vocabulary but writes only short, fragmented sentences.
Struggles with spacing between words and keeping letters on horizontal ruled lines.
context_questions: Does the learner complain of hand cramps or fatigue after 3 minutes of writing?
Is letter formation markedly improved on a tablet or keyboard?
How is the learner's posture and desk height relative to their seat?
alternative_explanations: Desk or chair size mismatch causing physical strain.
Inappropriate pencil thickness or friction on paper.
High cognitive burden of spelling interfering with fine-motor coordination.
things_to_try_now: Provide triangular pencil grips or softer writing implements.
Allow speech-to-text or oral transcription for expressive content.
Use raised-line paper to give tactile boundaries for letter sizing.
Separate the writing task into idea drafting first, handwriting second.
what_to_record: Length of continuous handwriting achieved before visible fatigue or pain.
Comparison of content depth between oral answers and written answers.
Pencil grip style and seating posture.
guides.how_to_judge: Compare sentence complexity and learner fatigue when using keyboard or oral response versus pen and paper.
guides.when_to_seek_help: If fine motor coordination or physical discomfort continues to hinder classroom access, consult an occupational therapist.
guides.non_diagnostic_statement: MINDTRACE gives educational observations, not diagnoses.

guides.title: Anxiety, sensory load, and environmental factors
guides.concern: A learner exhibits sudden drops in performance, freezing, or disengagement linked to stress or fatigue.
observable_behaviours: Shuts down, puts head on desk, or says 'I can't do this' before even reading the question.
Performance is strong in the first hour of school but drops steeply after lunch.
Shows physical signs of anxiety (fidgeting, breath holding, rapid heartbeat) during timed or public tasks.
context_questions: Did difficulty occur during a timed assessment or public reading in front of peers?
What was the noise and activity level in the classroom immediately beforehand?
Did the learner sleep well and have breakfast before school?
alternative_explanations: High cumulative cognitive fatigue from continuous processing.
Fear of peer embarrassment or negative evaluation.
Physical tiredness, illness, or unmet nutritional needs.
things_to_try_now: Remove all countdown timers and public read-aloud demands.
Offer a predictable 'pass' option where the learner can listen without penalty.
Incorporate a 3-minute quiet breathing or physical stretch break.
Break assessments into bite-sized 5-minute segments.
what_to_record: Times of day when disengagement or freezing occurs most frequently.
Difference in performance between untimed, quiet conditions and timed group settings.
Learner's self-reported comfort level when given advance notice.
guides.how_to_judge: Observe engagement and task willingness when timed pressure is removed over a 5-day cycle.
guides.when_to_seek_help: If anxiety or withdrawal significantly impairs daily functioning across school and home, consult a pastoral care lead or child psychologist.
guides.non_diagnostic_statement: MINDTRACE gives educational observations, not diagnoses.
